case_title: Tanua Rabidas v. State of Assam
accused_occupation: Assistant in the Social Welfare Department
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.326, s.34 (charged); conviction under IPC s.302
evidence_type: Dying declarations (two: oral statement and statement recorded by doctor), medical evidence (autopsy), eyewitness-type testimony of brother and neighbours, nurse's corroborating evidence
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; rigorous life imprisonment and fine of Rs.1,000 with default clause
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence affirmed
neutral_facts: On the anniversary of the couple's marriage, the accused and a co-accused were allegedly present in the house where the accused and the victim lived. It was alleged that the accused poured kerosene oil on his wife and set her on fire. She was taken to a mission hospital and then transferred to a medical college hospital, where she died of burn injuries. The victim's brother lodged the first information report, and the police investigated and filed a charge-sheet. The doctor who performed the autopsy opined that death was caused by shock from ante mortem flame burns covering about 90% of the body surface. At the hospital, a doctor examined the victim and recorded her statement that her husband had poured kerosene oil on her and ignited it, and a nurse attending her supported that account. A person who accompanied the victim's brother to the hospital testified that the victim had said in their presence that her husband had set her on fire. Neighbours heard a commotion and saw the victim near the gateway, as did a son of the accused from an earlier marriage. A maid servant present at the time could not be examined. Hair of the victim sent for chemical examination showed no smell of kerosene.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from shock due to ante mortem flame burns over about 90% of body surface (dermo-epidermal severity)
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declarations to PW-6 doctor and PW-7 nurse that the husband poured kerosene oil and set her on fire, corroborated by PW-1 (brother) and PW-8; autopsy evidence
witness_credibility: PW-6 and PW-7 had no prior contact with the victim, were not related to her and were not interested witnesses; their evidence was treated as very important and the Sessions Court found PW-6 true
trial_duration: offence: not given (victim examined by PW-6 on 04.12.1999); trial judgment: 30.03.2006; High Court: 20.03.2007; Supreme Court: 04.09.2014
legal_representation: Accused: P.K. Goswami, Parthiv K. Goswami, A. Henry, Rajiv Mehta (Senior Counsel P.K. Goswami). State: Avijit Roy (For Corporate Law Group)
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation carried out; charge-sheet filed; case committed to Sessions Court; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302, life imprisonment and Rs.1,000 fine. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction affirmed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: Case proved beyond reasonable doubt; evidence of PW-6 and PW-7 fully corroborated by PW-1 and PW-8
defence_argument: Ex.6 was allegedly an oral dying declaration and doubtful, as the victim with 90% burns may not have been able to speak; no smell of kerosene on the victim's body; PW-6 did not inform police of the dying declaration
legal_principle_applied: A dying declaration recorded by independent medical witnesses with no interest or prior acquaintance, corroborated by other evidence and free of any shown inducement, can sustain conviction; absence of kerosene smell in hair does not make it doubtful
precedent_relied_upon: State of Rajasthan v. Kishore (1996) 8 SCC 217 (relied on); Surinder Kumar v. State of Haryana (2011) 10 SCC 173 (distinguished)
